text: Dynamic and planar magnetic headphone drivers differ in how the diaphragm is pushed. A dynamic driver attaches a voice coil to a cone and sits it in a magnet gap, so current through the coil makes a force at that one spot and the cone carries the push out to its edges. A planar magnetic driver etches the conductor across a thin flat film hung between two magnet arrays, so the force lands evenly over the whole surface.

text: Point drive versus distributed drive barely matters at low frequencies, where a cone moves as one piston either way. The split shows up at high frequencies, where the wavelength inside the diaphragm gets short. A point-driven cone has to propagate that motion outward, so the rim lags the center and the surface stops moving as one piece and breaks into modes, while a flat film driven everywhere at once stays flat.
title: aadhar.sh: drivers

text: Cone breakup is a source of distortion. When different parts of a diaphragm move out of step, they radiate sound that was not in the signal, which shows up as resonance peaks and extra distortion in the treble. Spreading the drive across the whole diaphragm is how planar magnetic headphones keep distortion low at high frequencies.
title: aadhar.sh: drivers

text: A planar magnetic diaphragm can be extremely thin and light because it is driven everywhere at once and never has to be stiff enough to stay rigid under a point load. A dynamic cone, pushed only at the voice coil, has to resist bending, which sets a floor on its mass and stiffness.
title: aadhar.sh: drivers

text: Planar magnetic drivers are not universal because of tradeoffs. The magnet arrays are heavy and the large flat diaphragm is inefficient, so planars tend to be bigger, heavier on the head, and hungry for amplifier power. Dynamic drivers are light, cheap, efficient, and move a lot of air easily, which makes deep bass simple and lets them run off a phone, so most headphones in the world are dynamic.
title: aadhar.sh: drivers

text: The honest summary of planar versus dynamic: planar trades weight and power draw for low distortion, while dynamic trades some treble cleanliness for efficiency and easy bass. Neither wins outright. A well-engineered dynamic driver can sound excellent and a sloppy planar can sound worse than a good dynamic, because the mechanism sets the tendencies while the tuning and the build decide the result.

text: A planar magnetic (or magnetostatic) transducer drives a thin diaphragm with electrically conductive traces distributed across its surface, suspended in the field of arrays of permanent magnets on one or both sides. Because the conductor covers much of the diaphragm rather than concentrating at a single voice coil, the driving force is spread out and more uniform, which tends to lower distortion at the cost of low efficiency and heavy magnet structures.
